summary:
Same-sex relations are illegal in Eswatini for men and women throughout the country as of 12 March 2026. No legal gender recognition is available, so a trans visitor's passport and other identity documents are read exactly as issued, with no administrative route to align them with lived gender.

Eswatini recognises no same-sex relationships, and a trans visitor travelling in what would be locally classed as a same-sex relationship falls under the criminal law. In June 2012 Prime Minister Barnabas Sibusiso Dlamini said that people of the same sex could not even go to regional offices to get married and that the country was not ready to consider the question; in 2014 press secretary Percy Simelane said the government was monitoring the situation with a view to taking a legal position.

No registered national advocacy body exists to turn to for help. The registrar of companies refused to register Eswatini Sexual and Gender Minorities in June 2019 on the grounds of morality, and in April 2022 the High Court upheld that refusal while accepting that the constitution protects LGBTQ persons' rights to freedom of association, privacy and expression.

There is no broad legal protection against discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity in education, health, housing or employment. Section 4.3 of the 2013 National Policy on Sexual and Reproductive Health requires the Ministry of Health to make family planning information and services available regardless of sex, gender, age, status, sexual orientation and religion, and that is the level at which most of the country's protections operate.

The National Guidelines for Adolescent Sexual and Reproductive Health (2021) state that the right to equality includes freedom from discrimination because of one's sex or sexual orientation, define gender-based violence to include violence directed at a person based on gender identity or perceived adherence to norms of masculinity and femininity, and name LGBT people as a key population at higher risk of gender-based violence. The National Strategy to End Violence 2023-2027 lists sexual orientation or identity among its inclusivity principles, while the 2017 Broadcasting Guidelines Services and the 2022 Broadcasting (Content) Guidelines bar licensees from broadcasting material that sanctions, glamorises or incites violence or hatred on grounds including sexual orientation. None of these instruments supplies the general statutory right of action against discrimination that the statute books lack.

A 2019 survey found that 59% of LGBTQ respondents in the country had been discriminated against or treated disrespectfully at public health facilities and 30% had been denied healthcare services. That survey covers LGBTQ people generally rather than trans people specifically, and its fieldwork closed before 2020. Health programming has moved in the other direction: in February 2012 public health officials ran a Valentine's Day campaign urging gay people to test for HIV, and Deputy Director of Health Simon Zwane said the Health Ministry was extending HIV counselling and testing to same-sex couples, a step LGBTQ groups welcomed.

In March 2015 a 26-year-old lesbian woman from Nhlangano was murdered by a man who did not want to be in the presence of lesbians, and a few months earlier a gay man was murdered in the same town. The most recent documented case in this record is from 2015; no later instance is documented.

Some traditional, religious and government officials have criticised same-sex sexual conduct as neither morally Swati nor Christian, according to the US State Department's 2021 country report. In 2012 former Foreign Affairs Minister Mgwagwa Gamedze rejected a UN working group call for an LGBTQ protection law, saying that so few gay people lived in Eswatini that drafting one was not worth the effort; in May 2017 the UN Human Rights Committee pressed the government on measures to protect people from discrimination and violence based on sexual orientation and gender identity.
tangentialFactors:
Freedom House's Freedom in the World 2024 rates Eswatini Not Free with an overall score of 17 out of 100, comprising 1 out of 40 for political rights and 16 out of 60 for civil liberties, describing an absolute monarchy with severely restricted civic space. The 2024 BTI country report places the refusal to register LGBTQ+ groups inside a wider pattern of restricted political formations, meetings and recruitment, noting that 'Mswati must fall' had become a common protest slogan.

Public LGBT visibility has nonetheless been documented. The first Eswatini Pride was declared a great success in July 2018, and in June 2021 LGBTQI+ persons conducted a virtual Pride celebration without incident. In December 2018 a church welcoming LGBTIQ people reopened, recorded alongside a finding of no let-up on discrimination in the kingdom.

A 2013 survey reported that 43% of lesbian and transgender respondents had attempted suicide in the past year and 78% regularly used intoxicating substances to feel normal. The figure combines lesbian and transgender respondents and its window closed in 2013; no later measurement of this kind appears in the record.
localsOnly:
Same-sex couples are prohibited from adopting children, while prospective heterosexual adoptive parents may be single, married or divorced.

Rock of Hope states that with no legislation recognising LGBTIs or protecting gender identity, LGBTQ people cannot be open about their orientation or gender identity for fear of rejection and discrimination, and that most choose to remain in the closet or move to South Africa.

The 2021 National Social Security Policy defines equity as free from discrimination including sexual orientation, a policy-level commitment that stops short of the statutory protections absent from education, health, housing and employment.
outOfScopeNotes:
No source in this inventory addresses entry procedures, visa issuance, document-marker treatment or screening practice at Eswatini's borders for trans travellers, including whether gender presentation triggers secondary screening or an anatomy inspection. That question is unresolved here.

The record contains no trans-specific violence statistic with a denominator. The documented killings it holds are of a lesbian woman in March 2015 and a gay man in the same town a few months earlier, both above the general pattern only insofar as the sources describe them as bias-motivated; no per-capita comparison and no trans-specific figure is available.

The 2019 health-facility survey measures LGBTQ respondents as a whole and the 2013 survey merges lesbian and transgender respondents, so neither isolates trans people's experience. The most recent of the two closed before 2020, and neither can be read as current prevalence.

The sources date the refusal to register the LGBTI group to June 2019, while the report documenting it appeared in July 2019; the record does not resolve which month the decision itself was taken. Entry, exit and document-gender questions are otherwise not sourced at all.
